title: H is for Hawk
author: Helen Macdonald
blurb: A grieving woman meets her goshawk for the first time. Mythical imagery and physical description capture a life-changing moment.
source: Macdonald meets her goshawk for the first time
heading: From H is for Hawk - Helen Macdonald
context: When Macdonald's father died suddenly of a heart attack, Macdonald was devastated. An experienced falconer, she adopted a goshawk to distract her from her grief. In this extract Macdonald meets her hawk for the first time.

paragraphs.html: 'We'll check the ring numbers against the Article 10s,' he explained, pulling a sheaf of yellow paper from the rucksack and unfolding two of the official forms that accompany captive-bred rare birds throughout their lives. 'Don't want you going home with the wrong bird.'

We noted the numbers. We stared down at the boxes, at their parcel-tape handles, their doors of thin plywood and hinges of carefully tied string. Then he knelt on the concrete, untied a hinge on the smaller box and squinted into its dark interior. A sudden thump of feathered shoulders and the box shook as if someone had punched it, hard, from within. 'She's got her hood off,' he said, and frowned. That light, leather hood was to keep the hawk from fearful sights. Like us.

Another hinge untied. Concentration. Infinite caution. Daylight irrigating the box. Scratching talons, another thump. And another. Thump. The air turned syrupy, slow, flecked with dust. The last few seconds before a battle. And with the last bow pulled free, he reached inside, and amidst a whirring, chaotic clatter of wings and feet and talons and a high-pitched twittering and it's all happening at once, the man pulls an enormous, enormous hawk out of the box and in a strange coincidence of world and deed a great flood of sunlight drenches us and everything is brilliance and fury. The hawk's wings, barred and beating, the sharp fingers of her dark-tipped primaries cutting the air, her feathers raised like the scattered quills of a fretful porpentine. Two enormous eyes. My heart jumps sideways. She is a conjuring trick. A reptile. A fallen angel. A griffon from the pages of an illuminated bestiary. Something bright and distant, like gold falling through water. A broken marionette of wings, legs and light-splashed feathers. She is wearing jesses, and the man holds them. For one awful, long moment she is hanging head-downward, wings open, like a turkey in a butcher's shop, only her head is turned right-way-up and she is seeing more than she has ever seen before in her whole short life. Her world was an aviary no larger than a living room. Then it was a box. But now it is this; and she can see everything: the point-source glitter on the waves, a diving cormorant a hundred yards out; pigment flakes under wax on the lines of parked cars; far hills and the heather on them and miles and miles of sky where the sun spreads on dust and water and illegible things moving in it that are white scraps of gulls. Everything startling and new-stamped on her entirely astonished brain.

Through all this the man was perfectly calm. He gathered up the hawk in one practised movement, folding her wings, anchoring her broad feathered back against his chest, gripping her scaled yellow legs in one hand. 'Let's get that hood back on,' he said tautly. There was concern in his face. It was born of care. This hawk had been hatched in an incubator, had broken from a frail bluish eggshell into a humid perspex box, and for the first few days of her life this man had fed her with scraps of meat held in a pair of tweezers, waiting patiently for the lumpen, fluffy chick to notice the food and eat, her new neck wobbling with the effort of keeping her head in the air. All at once I loved this man, and fiercely. I grabbed the hood from the box and turned to the hawk. Her beak was open, her hackles raised; her wild eyes were the colour of sun on white paper, and they stared because the whole world had fallen into them at once. One, two, three. I tucked the hood over her head. There was a brief intimation of a thin, angular skull under her feathers, of an alien brain fizzing and fusing with terror, then I drew the braces closed. We checked the ring numbers against the form.
It was the wrong bird. This was the younger one. The smaller one. This was not my hawk.

So we put her back and opened the other box, which was meant to hold the larger, older bird. And dear God, it did. Everything about this second hawk was different. She came out like a Victorian melodrama: a sort of madwoman in the attack. She was smokier and darker and much, much bigger, and instead of twittering, she wailed; great, awful gouts of sound like a thing in pain, and the sound was unbearable. This is my hawk, I was telling myself and it was all I could do to breathe. She too was bareheaded, and I grabbed the hood from the box as before. But as I brought it up to her face I looked into her eyes and saw something blank and crazy in her stare. Some madness from a distant country. I didn't recognise her. This isn't my hawk. The hood was on, the ring numbers checked, the bird back in the box, the yellow form folded, the money exchanged, and all I could think was, But this isn't my hawk. Slow panic. I knew what I had to say, and it was a monstrous breach of etiquette. 'This is really awkward,' I began. 'But I really liked the first one. Do you think there's any chance I could take that one instead . . .?' I tailed off. His eyebrows were raised. I started again, saying stupider things: 'I'm sure the other falconer would like the larger bird? She's more beautiful than the first one, isn't she? I know this is out of order, but I ... Could I? Would it be all right, do you think?' And on and on, a desperate, crazy barrage of incoherent appeals.

I'm sure nothing I said persuaded him more than the look on my face as I said it. A tall, white-faced woman with wind-wrecked hair and exhausted eyes was pleading with him on a quayside, hands held out as if she were in a seaside production of Medea. Looking at me he must have sensed that my stuttered request wasn't a simple one. That there was something behind it that was very important. There was a moment of total silence.

wrong-bird.quote: Don't want you going home with the wrong bird
wrong-bird.what: The handler jokes about the wrong bird, which is exactly what Macdonald later fears she has.
wrong-bird.effect: It plants the question we carry throughout: which hawk is the right one?

parcel-tape.what: 'Parcel-tape' handles are the stuff of any ordinary delivery.
parcel-tape.effect: The cheap packaging makes the wild creature inside seem even more startling.

thin-plywood.quote: thin plywood and hinges of carefully tied string
thin-plywood.what: 'Thin' and 'string' stress how flimsy the boxes are, though 'carefully tied' shows care.
thin-plywood.effect: Only a fragile wall holds back something powerful, so tension rises before we see her.

thump-feathered.what: We hear the hawk before we see her, as 'feathered shoulders' slam the box.
thump-feathered.effect: She feels heavy and close yet still hidden, which makes us more anxious.

punched-it.what: The box shakes as if punched, and the commas around 'hard' make the blow land.
punched-it.effect: The human image shows her strength and hints that she is angry at being trapped.

keep-hawk.quote: keep the hawk from fearful sights. Like us
keep-hawk.what: The dry two-word fragment 'Like us.' adds the humans to the list of 'fearful sights'.
keep-hawk.effect: We suddenly see the scene through the hawk's eyes, where the people are the threat.

concentration-caution.what: These minor sentences (sentences with no verb) read like quick notes in her head.
concentration-caution.effect: The full stops force pauses, so time slows into nervous stillness before the box opens.

daylight-irrigating.what: 'Irrigating' means watering dry land, so daylight seems to flow into the box like water.
daylight-irrigating.effect: The dark box fills slowly, as if the hawk is entering a new, living world.

thump-repetition.what: After 'another thump. And another.', the lone 'Thump.' makes each sentence shorter than the last.
thump-repetition.effect: The shrinking beats sound like a pounding heart, tightening tension until something must break.

syrupy-slow.what: 'Syrupy' makes air thick and 'flecked with dust' makes it visible: synaesthesia (mixing the senses).
syrupy-slow.effect: Time seems to slow, as it does in moments of shock.

last-seconds.quote: The last few seconds before a battle
last-seconds.what: Comparing the moment to 'before a battle' turns opening a box into a scene of war.
last-seconds.effect: We brace for violence and feel how huge this meeting is to her.

whirring-chaotic.quote: whirring, chaotic clatter of wings and feet and talons and a high-pitched twittering
whirring-chaotic.what: Polysyndeton (repeating 'and') makes the list of sounds rush on without a break.
whirring-chaotic.effect: Noise hits us from every side, too fast to pick apart, just as it hit her.

all-happening.what: The past tense ('he reached') suddenly switches to the present ('it's all happening', 'pulls').
all-happening.effect: We are dropped into the moment, and the chatty phrase sounds like her breathless voice.

enormous-enormous.what: Macdonald repeats 'enormous', too amazed to reach for a better word.
enormous-enormous.effect: The childlike repetition makes the hawk seem too big for ordinary language.

flood-sunlight.quote: a great flood of sunlight drenches us and everything is brilliance and fury
flood-sunlight.what: Sunlight 'drenches' them at that exact moment, a 'strange coincidence' that feels like the world answering the hawk.
flood-sunlight.effect: 'Brilliance and fury' pairs beauty with danger, which sums up the hawk.

barred-beating.what: The hard, repeated 'b' sound copies the beat of the striped ('barred') wings.
barred-beating.effect: We hear the wings move as well as see them.

sharp-fingers.quote: sharp fingers of her dark-tipped primaries cutting the air
sharp-fingers.what: The wing-tip feathers ('primaries') become 'sharp fingers' that are 'cutting the air'.
sharp-fingers.effect: The wings seem like hands holding knives, skilful and dangerous.

heart-jumps.what: Hearts usually 'jump' with fright or joy, but 'sideways' makes the feeling odd and off-balance.
heart-jumps.effect: The short, present-tense sentence lets us feel the jolt as it happens.

conjuring-trick.quote: a conjuring trick. A reptile. A fallen angel. A griffon from the pages of an illuminated bestiary
conjuring-trick.what: Four quick metaphors pull different ways: magic, 'reptile', 'fallen angel', 'griffon' (half eagle, half lion).
conjuring-trick.effect: The hawk is too strange for one description, so Macdonald keeps trying.

gold-falling.quote: Something bright and distant, like gold falling through water
gold-falling.what: 'Gold falling through water' is precious and shining, yet sinking out of reach.
gold-falling.effect: Something precious slipping away may echo Macdonald's grief for her father.

hanging-turkey.quote: hanging head-downward, wings open, like a turkey in a butcher's shop
hanging-turkey.what: Soon after the angel and griffon, the hawk becomes 'a turkey in a butcher's shop'.
hanging-turkey.effect: The drop to dead meat is a shock: she is a fragile, real animal.

seeing-more.quote: she is seeing more than she has ever seen before in her whole short life
seeing-more.what: Macdonald moves inside the hawk's mind, and 'whole short life' reminds us how young she is.
seeing-more.effect: Her shock at the huge world makes her seem vulnerable after the fierce images.

but-now.what: Her world shrinks from aviary to box, then 'this' throws it wide open.
but-now.effect: The vague 'this' suggests a new world too big to name.

point-source.what: 'Point-source' is a scientific-sounding term for light from single tiny points.
point-source.effect: The exact wording shows how sharply the hawk sees each glint on the sea.

pigment-flakes.what: The hawk sees 'pigment flakes' (tiny bits of colour) under the polish on parked cars.
pigment-flakes.effect: No human would see this, so we realise how overwhelming the world must look to her.

miles-sky.what: Repeating 'miles and miles' stretches the phrase out, just as the sky stretches out.
miles-sky.effect: After a small aviary and a box, we feel both the freedom and the shock.

illegible-things.quote: illegible things moving in it that are white scraps of gulls
illegible-things.what: 'Illegible' means impossible to read: the gulls are shapes before they are named.
illegible-things.effect: We see as the hawk does, a world she has not yet learned to understand.

everything-startling.quote: Everything startling and new-stamped on her entirely astonished brain
everything-startling.what: 'New-stamped' suggests each sight is pressed into her brain, like a design stamped on a new coin.
everything-startling.effect: These first impressions will stay with her for good.

perfectly-calm.what: After the chaos, the new paragraph opens with the handler 'perfectly calm', instantly changing the pace.
perfectly-calm.effect: His steadiness makes Macdonald's racing feelings stand out.

one-practised.what: 'Practised' shows long experience, and the verbs 'folding', 'anchoring', 'gripping' are smooth and controlled.
one-practised.effect: In a few words the wild, flapping hawk is safe in his hands.

scaled-yellow.what: 'Scaled' legs echo her earlier metaphor 'A reptile.'
scaled-yellow.effect: Birds come from ancient reptile ancestors, so the hawk seems old, wild and a little alien.

tautly.what: 'Tautly' means stretched tight, like a rope.
tautly.effect: One word reveals the worry hidden behind his calm actions.

concern-care.quote: concern in his face. It was born of care
concern-care.what: 'Born of care' leads straight into the story of the hawk's hatching.
concern-care.effect: His worry is love, built up by raising this bird from her first days.

frail-bluish.what: A flashback to the hatching, where 'frail' and 'bluish' make the eggshell delicate and small.
frail-bluish.effect: The fierce hawk was once helpless, which makes us protective and explains the handler's care.

lumpen-fluffy.what: 'Lumpen' (heavy and shapeless) beside 'fluffy' paints an awkward, soft baby bird.
lumpen-fluffy.effect: The terrifying hawk was once comic and helpless, which makes us fond of her.

wobbling-effort.what: Even holding up her head is hard work for the chick.
wobbling-effort.effect: We feel tender towards her, and see how patiently the handler watched over her.

all-once-loved.quote: All at once I loved this man, and fiercely
all-once-loved.what: 'And fiercely' comes after a comma, so the strongest word lands last.
all-once-loved.effect: Grief has left her raw, so his kindness to the hawk moves her deeply.

hackles-raised.what: 'Hackles' are neck feathers, and raising them with an open beak shows fear and aggression.
hackles-raised.effect: We picture a terrified animal on the edge, ready to strike.

colour-sun.quote: colour of sun on white paper
colour-sun.what: The eyes are the exact pale, glaring yellow of sunlight on white paper.
colour-sun.effect: We almost feel the glare, as if the eyes are full of the light pouring in.

world-fallen.quote: the whole world had fallen into them at once
world-fallen.what: Normally we look out at the world, but here it 'had fallen into' her eyes.
world-fallen.effect: 'At once' shows it all arriving in one crushing rush that she cannot control.

thin-angular.what: Hooding her, Macdonald feels a 'thin, angular skull' ('intimation' means a faint hint).
thin-angular.effect: For a moment we feel how breakable the fierce creature is underneath.

alien-brain.quote: alien brain fizzing and fusing with terror
alien-brain.what: 'Fizzing and fusing' makes the brain sound like wiring about to blow, with a crackling 'f' sound.
alien-brain.effect: 'Alien' reminds us we can never fully know the hawk's terror.

wrong-bird-reveal.what: After a long, rich paragraph, this flat five-word sentence echoes the handler's opening joke.
wrong-bird-reveal.effect: The jolt hits hard: all that wonder was spent on the wrong hawk.

not-my-hawk.what: Flat facts ('younger', 'smaller') lead to the rule: this bird belongs to someone else.
not-my-hawk.effect: The plain tone hides disappointment, since she has just fallen for this hawk.

oh.what: The whole paragraph is one small word, surrounded by white space.
oh.effect: Her disappointment is too big for more words, so the blank space speaks for her.

dear-god.what: 'Dear God' bursts into the sentence like speech.
dear-god.effect: We hear her shock, and know this second hawk will be even more overwhelming.

victorian-melodrama.quote: Victorian melodrama: a sort of madwoman in the attack
victorian-melodrama.what: This allusion twists 'madwoman in the attic', the locked-up Bertha Mason in Jane Eyre.
victorian-melodrama.effect: The pun casts the hawk as a wild, trapped woman breaking free, and lightens the mood.

smokier-darker.quote: smokier and darker and much, much bigger
smokier-darker.what: Three comparatives joined by 'and', then 'much, much', make her grow as we read.
smokier-darker.effect: 'Smokier' gives her a shadowy, menacing look beside the first hawk.

wailed.what: The first hawk twittered; this one 'wailed', a human sound of grief.
wailed.effect: Her cry mirrors Macdonald's own grief, which may be why it is so hard to bear.

great-awful.quote: great, awful gouts of sound like a thing in pain
great-awful.what: 'Gouts' usually means spurts of blood, but here it describes sound.
great-awful.effect: The noise feels like it pours from a wound, and we almost flinch.

unbearable.what: The sentence builds to one heavy word about how the sound makes her feel.
unbearable.effect: An experienced falconer finding a hawk's cry 'unbearable' suggests it touches her own grief.

this-my-hawk.what: 'I was telling myself' shows she has to work to believe what the paperwork says.
this-my-hawk.effect: Her heart has not caught up with the facts.

all-could-breathe.quote: it was all I could do to breathe
all-could-breathe.what: Her emotion becomes physical, in plain, everyday words.
all-could-breathe.effect: We feel her panic in our own bodies as even breathing becomes hard.

blank-crazy.quote: blank and crazy in her stare
blank-crazy.what: 'Blank' suggests nothing inside and 'crazy' too much: a paradox (two ideas that seem to clash).
blank-crazy.effect: Looking for a connection, she finds a mind closed to her.

some-madness.quote: Some madness from a distant country
some-madness.what: This minor sentence (no main verb) places her madness in 'a distant country'.
some-madness.effect: The hawk's wildness belongs somewhere Macdonald cannot reach or understand.

didnt-recognise.what: She 'didn't recognise' a bird she has never met, as if expecting to know her hawk.
didnt-recognise.effect: So soon after losing her father, she seems to crave a deep bond.

isnt-my-hawk.what: 'My hawk' keeps returning, now as a present-tense denial.
isnt-my-hawk.effect: Her mind is going round in circles, and the thought strikes her as she looks.

but-isnt.what: A long list of finished jobs ('the money exchanged') runs against one stuck thought.
but-isnt.effect: The world moves on while she is frozen, so her protest feels more desperate.

slow-panic.what: Panic is usually sudden, so 'slow panic' is an oxymoron (two opposite ideas together).
slow-panic.effect: We feel dread rising bit by bit as she works up to speaking.

monstrous-breach.what: 'Breach of etiquette' means breaking polite rules, and 'monstrous' exaggerates it with self-mocking humour.
monstrous-breach.effect: She wants the first hawk badly enough to embarrass herself.

desperate-barrage.quote: desperate, crazy barrage of incoherent appeals
desperate-barrage.what: A 'barrage' is a burst of gunfire; 'incoherent' means making no sense.
desperate-barrage.effect: Her honesty about losing control makes us trust her and shows grief stripping away her composure.

tall-white.quote: tall, white-faced woman with wind-wrecked hair and exhausted eyes
tall-white.what: She describes herself in the third person, worn down by 'wind-wrecked' hair and 'exhausted' eyes.
tall-white.effect: Seen from outside, her grief is written on her face for the handler to read.

seaside-medea.what: Medea, from Greek tragedy, kills her own children out of rage and revenge.
seaside-medea.effect: The grand comparison shows how wild she looks, while 'seaside' lets her laugh at herself.

something-behind.quote: something behind it that was very important
something-behind.what: Macdonald never says what lies 'behind it', but we know about her father's death.
something-behind.effect: We understand what the handler can only guess: the hawk matters because of her grief.

moment-silence.quote: There was a moment of total silence
moment-silence.what: The extract ends on silence, before we hear the handler's answer.
moment-silence.effect: We are left waiting with Macdonald, holding her hope and fear.

porpentine.note: Shakespeare uses it in Hamlet: 'quills upon the fretful porpentine'. Macdonald echoes that line.
porpentine.effect: The old word makes the hawk sound like a creature from an ancient story, her feathers bristling like spines.

bestiary.meaning: A medieval book describing animals, real and imaginary.
bestiary.note: Bestiaries were often 'illuminated' (decorated with gold and bright colours). Each animal came with a moral lesson.
bestiary.effect: Putting the hawk in this kind of book makes her seem legendary, a creature from myth.

marionette.meaning: A puppet worked by strings from above.
marionette.note: The hawk dangles from her jesses while the man holds them, like a puppet on strings.
marionette.effect: Her movements look jerky and out of her control. Someone else is holding the strings.

jesses.meaning: Leather straps fitted to a hawk's legs.
jesses.note: A falconry term. The handler holds the jesses to keep control of the bird.
jesses.effect: The correct technical word shows Macdonald's expertise as a falconer and makes the scene feel real.

overview.heading: Why Macdonald wrote this
overview.intro: She has several aims in this extract.

points.label: To capture a turning point
points.text: "But now it is this" shows a life changing in an instant, for the hawk and, we sense, for Macdonald.

points.label: To explore grief
points.text: "something behind it that was very important" hints that the hawk is bound up with her grief for her father.

points.label: To show a desperate need
points.text: "monstrous breach of etiquette" shows she will break the rules to get the hawk she feels is hers.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: She writes for several kinds of reader.

points.label: Readers new to falconry
points.text: "jesses" and "hackles" appear in clear context, so readers who know nothing about hawks can still follow.

points.label: Readers who know grief
points.text: "it was all I could do to breathe" shows a panic that anyone who has lost someone may recognise.

points.label: Lovers of nature writing
points.text: "pigment flakes under wax" shows the close, careful detail these readers enjoy.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her voice shifts as the scene unfolds.

points.label: Nervous excitement
points.text: "My heart jumps sideways" shows a physical jolt of nerves at the first sight of the hawk.

points.label: Awestruck wonder
points.text: "enormous, enormous" shows her so amazed that she repeats herself.

points.label: Fierce emotion
points.text: "All at once I loved this man, and fiercely" shows feeling arriving suddenly and strongly.

points.label: Desperate pleading
points.text: "desperate, crazy barrage" shows her losing control, and her honesty about it.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Her imagery makes us see the hawk with fresh eyes.

points.label: Mythical comparisons
points.text: "A reptile. A fallen angel. A griffon" shows a hawk too strange for any one description.

points.label: Mixing the senses
points.text: "syrupy, slow" makes the air thick enough to touch, so time seems to slow down.

points.label: Precise observation
points.text: "pigment flakes under wax" shows how much more sharply the hawk sees than we do.

points.label: Literary allusion
points.text: "seaside production of Medea" compares her to a tragic heroine, with a touch of self-mocking humour.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The structure builds tension, then drops it suddenly.

points.label: Slow build-up
points.text: "Concentration. Infinite caution" uses short fragments to slow time before the box opens.

points.label: Moment of change
points.text: "But now it is this" marks the instant the hawk's small world bursts open.

points.label: One-word paragraph
points.text: "Oh." shows a disappointment too big for more words.

points.label: Cliffhanger ending
points.text: "moment of total silence" leaves us waiting for the handler's answer.
